title: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
desc: Separates isolated answers, extended workflows and human ratings while requiring diagnostic metrics, cost controls and agent attribution.

kps.k: The cluster concerns what AI evaluations actually measure: answer quality, human preference and successful professional workflows require distinct tests.
kps.d: AI Agents That Matter argues that model-evaluation frameworks do not suffice for agents. A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents extends the target from textual outputs to sequential decisions in changing environments. Zheng and colleagues show a different measurement gap: conventional benchmark scores can miss chatbot improvements that users prefer, so they present preference-based and traditional benchmarks as complementary. These arguments support matching evaluation to the intended use, not treating a single score as a general measure of competence.

qs.q: Our thesis is that agents are sufficiently different from models that benchmarking practices need to be rethought.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Such evaluation must go beyond measuring LLM textual outputs to assess an agent’s capacity for sequential decision-making and operation within dynamic environments.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Realistic, extended tasks expose capability gaps that isolated answer tests can miss.
kps.d: The supplied April 2026 agent-evaluation survey reports stronger short-term than long-horizon planning in PlanBench and continuing difficulties with interleaved tasks and memory consistency. It reports performance below 25% Pass@1 in its discussion of SWE-bench Pro; this is a cited benchmark result, not a universal estimate of agent capability. Agent-as-a-Judge likewise distinguishes simple function correctness and competition-style coding sophistication from real development workflows. TheAgentCompany adds occupational relevance, interfaces, intermediate checkpoints and interaction with other agents as separate comparison dimensions, without supplying performance results.

qs.q: PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023) provides a comprehensive evaluation framework specifically designed to assess planning capabilities in LLM agents across diverse domains, revealing that current models excel at short-term tactical planning but struggle with strategic long-horizon planning.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: While these benchmarks are useful for evaluating the correctness of generated code, they are limited in complexity and do not fully represent the challenges encountered in real-world software development.
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

kps.k: LLM judges offer scalable preference assessment, but agreement with people does not establish expert correctness.
kps.d: Zheng and colleagues report over 80% agreement between strong LLM judges such as GPT-4 and controlled or crowdsourced human preferences, comparable to agreement between humans in their evaluations. They also identify position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and limited reasoning. Agent-as-a-Judge proposes more nuanced automated judgment, but its supplied excerpts contain no results for its own approach. The substantive tension is between scalable assessment and evaluator validity, rather than a demonstrated conflict between equally comprehensive studies. The supplied material does not establish that conversational preference agreement transfers to high-stakes legal judgment.

qs.q: Our results reveal that strong LLM judges                                                       like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well,                                                       achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans.
qs.a: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Our work builds on these advancements by exploring how LLMs can perform more nuanced judgment tasks, further investigating their potential in decision-making across various domains.
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Rubric formats and evaluation protocols impose important limits on score interpretation.
kps.d: RubricEval restricts its study to binary rubric-level judgments, excludes Likert-scale and comparative judgments, and acknowledges possible exclusion of genuinely hard cases. It therefore cannot establish superiority across evaluation formats. The DeepSeek-R1 evaluation excerpt describes judging only final summaries to limit length bias and changing selected prompts to zero-shot because few-shot chain-of-thought may hurt performance; it does not quantify either effect. Bibliographic coverage in JudgmentBench, JADE and related papers identifies rubric validity, fairness and statistical assessment as research topics, not demonstrated solutions.

kps.k: Useful comparisons need cost controls, diagnostic metrics and separation of model capability from agent design.
kps.d: AI Agents That Matter recommends cost-controlled comparisons, separate model and downstream evaluations, appropriate hold-outs and standardized practices. The agent-evaluation survey recommends independently varying the backbone model, surrounding harness and memory or planning modules to identify the source of gains. It also argues that end-to-end success can conceal intermediate errors and calls for trajectory metrics alongside token use, API expense and inference time. Its safety recommendations add adversarial robustness, bias and policy compliance rather than assuming task completion establishes safe operation.

qs.q: We have taken the first steps toward a principled approach to agent benchmarking, resulting in recommendations including cost-controlled comparisons, separating model and downstream evaluation, preventing shortcuts using appropriate hold-outs, and greater standardization of evaluation practices.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Future work should develop controlled evaluation protocols that vary each factor independently, enabling systematic comparison and isolating the contribution of individual components, whether LLM capabilities, harness design, or specific modules such as memory or planning, to overall agent performance.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Benchmark credibility depends on maintenance and retirement, not just initial construction.
kps.d: BetterBench calls for bug fixes, user-feedback updates and continued assessment of relevance after release. It identifies saturation, declining task relevance and better alternatives as reasons for retirement, with archived data, code and documentation and clear retirement labels. Saturation means reaching a metric’s ceiling, not mastering the corresponding real-world work. The agent-evaluation survey similarly recommends adapting benchmarks to changing tools and repairing defective tests, while choosing benchmarks that fit the deployment environment.

qs.q: Once the benchmark and its documentation are released, developers must conduct regular maintenance to ensure ongoing usability.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: These ongoing adaptations serve several purposes: matching the increased capabilities of agents, addressing shortcomings of previous versions (e.g., by conducting human verification and refining success metrics), and adapting to evolving research ecosystems such as MCP-based tool calling.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The supplied evidence supports methodological guidance, but few conclusions about legal deployment or economic impact.
kps.d: Much of the material consists only of bibliographies, including the supplied LegalBench, legal-research reliability, legal-rubric, developer-productivity and economic-evaluation excerpts. These do not establish the named papers’ findings or endorse cited claims. PRBench supplies an evaluation setting with web search and code execution, not results; the privileged-information grading paper supplies only a title-level performance assertion. Consequently, this cluster does not demonstrate legal-tool reliability, productivity gains, labour substitution or the replacement of human verification. Its practical contribution is to specify what stronger, use-specific evaluation would need to establish.

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources cannot be assigned a substantive position on the cluster’s proposition. Across the supplied records, the common limitation is evidentiary: most excerpts are bibliography entries that identify relevant topics—rubric versus preference evaluation, LLM judges, legal and specialist benchmarks, agent tasks, evaluator bias, and governance risks—but do not provide the sources’ own methods, findings or recommendations. PRBench differs slightly by directly stating that it examines chat models equipped with web search and code-interpreter tools, yet the excerpt reports no results and does not show whether its evaluation distinguishes isolated answer quality, human preference and extended professional-workflow success. Material variation therefore lies in subject emphasis rather than position: JudgmentBench and LeMAJ foreground judging methods; GDPval and Xpertbench reference real-world or agent tasks; the governance source cites behavioural and security concerns. None establishes acceptance, extension or rejection of the proposition’s requirements for use-specific tests, diagnostic metrics, cost controls, benchmark maintenance or attribution of performance between the model and agent design. This finding concerns only the curated sources and does not characterize legal-tech vendors generally.

vlens.an: The curated sources in this professional voice are thematically aligned with the proposition but do not provide enough substantive evidence to establish a collective position. Every supplied excerpt is bibliography-only, so cited titles cannot be treated as findings, recommendations or endorsements by NIST, the statistical-evaluation paper, LexRubric or the interdisciplinary review. Collectively, the references touch many of the proposition’s concerns: construct validity and human-preference evaluation; agent and legal-domain benchmarks; professional-needs alignment; contamination, nondeterminism and statistical uncertainty; and holistic or sociotechnical evaluation. There is material variation in emphasis: NIST’s references foreground agent capabilities, evaluation infrastructure and contamination; Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox foregrounds validity and statistical reliability; LexRubric foregrounds legal tasks and expert rubrics; and Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? ranges more broadly across professional needs, safety, auditability and sociotechnical context. However, none of the supplied material reveals whether these sources themselves accept the proposition’s distinctions among isolated answer quality, human preference and extended professional-workflow success, or support its specific requirements for diagnostic metrics, cost controls, agent attribution and benchmark maintenance. The appropriate position is therefore Unclear, rather than Supports or Builds on.

vlens.an: The attributable academia-and-research evidence accepts the proposition’s core distinction between what different evaluations measure and materially extends it into a broader methodology for credible AI assessment. Sources distinguish conventional benchmark performance from human preference, and isolated textual correctness from successful long-horizon workflows. They then add concrete requirements: intermediate checkpoint and trajectory metrics, workplace-relevant tasks and interfaces, cost-controlled comparisons, hold-outs, separation of backbone-model capability from agent-harness design, safety testing, and benchmark maintenance and retirement. Internal variation concerns emphasis rather than direction. Zheng and colleagues focus on scalable measurement of human chatbot preferences while warning that judge bias and limited reasoning constrain interpretation; agent-benchmark researchers focus on workflow realism, diagnostic attribution and operational cost; RubricEval and the DeepSeek-R1 evaluation illustrate how rubric format, prompt choice and bias controls bound score interpretation; BetterBench adds benchmark lifecycle governance. Some contributions state proposed methods without supplying validating results, so these are methodological extensions rather than demonstrated guarantees of evaluator validity. A substantial portion of the supplied corpus is bibliography-only or fragmentary and therefore remains indeterminate; its topical relevance cannot be treated as endorsement. Because the sources are curated, this synthesis characterises the supplied professional voice and does not imply prevalence across academia or research generally.

elens.an: The sole curated source assigned to the 2015–2022 automation-debate period provides no substantive argument, findings, or recommendations in the supplied excerpts. Bibliographic references, an appendix heading, and an unfinished etymological sentence do not show whether it accepts the proposition that preferences, answer correctness, and professional-workflow success require distinct evaluations with diagnostic metrics, cost controls, and agent attribution. There is therefore no evidentiary basis for identifying common reasons or material internal variation within this period; nor should this single, evidentially incomplete source be treated as representative of the broader automation debate.

The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction between conventional model scores, human preference and realistic workflow performance, and materially extend it with concrete evaluation practices. Zheng and colleagues show that preference-oriented and traditional benchmarks are complementary rather than interchangeable, while also limiting LLM judges to scalable approximations of preference because of bias and reasoning weaknesses. Agent-focused sources develop the workflow side: AI Agents That Matter calls for separate model and downstream evaluations, cost-controlled comparisons, hold-outs and standardisation; TheAgentCompany adds occupational relevance, interface access, intermediate checkpoints and multi-agent interaction; and Agent-as-a-Judge argues that isolated code-correctness tests do not represent real software-development challenges. BetterBench further extends the proposition across the benchmark lifecycle through maintenance and retirement criteria. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and evidential strength: some sources primarily address preference measurement, others agent workflows or benchmark governance, and several offer design proposals or comparison dimensions without validating them through reported results. Bibliography-only excerpts provide no determinable position. No supplied substantive source rejects the proposition, but the corpus is curated and the source count should not be read as evidence of broader prevalence.

elens.an: The substantive evidence aligned with this adoption-at-scale facet accepts the cluster’s core proposition that evaluation must be matched to what is being measured rather than reduced to a single benchmark score. It materially develops that proposition by specifying workflow-level tests for sequential decisions in dynamic environments, trajectory diagnostics for intermediate failures, operational-cost metrics, benchmark maintenance, safety testing, and controlled attribution among the backbone model, agent harness and modules. The DeepSeek-R1 material also supports separating standard benchmark evaluation from LLM-judged open-ended generation and shows that results depend on protocol choices intended to limit length bias and on benchmark-specific prompting. Internal variation is primarily evidential rather than oppositional: most supplied excerpts are bibliographies or title-level fragments, so they establish topical relevance but not their sources’ positions or findings; PRBench supplies only an evaluation setting. No substantive source clearly rejects the proposition. A temporal qualification is necessary because the most developed contribution is identified as an April 2026 revision even though it is included in the 2025 facet. Given the curated nature of the corpus, this assessment characterises only the supplied sources and does not indicate prevalence across researchers or adopters.

elens.an: The current-wave (2026) evidence does not establish a clear collective position on the proposition. Most supplied excerpts are bibliographies or fragments that merely identify research on construct validity, evaluator bias, legal and agent benchmarks, ecological validity, statistical uncertainty and real-world tasks. Those topics are consistent with the proposition’s concerns, but citation does not show that the source itself accepts or develops the distinction among human preference, professional correctness and workflow success. The principal internal variation is RubricEval, whose substantive limitations passage supports protocol-specific interpretation: it confines itself to binary rubric-level judgments, excludes other formats and acknowledges that difficult cases may be omitted. That is direct but narrow support for one component of the proposition; it does not address extended professional workflows, cost controls or attribution of performance between the model and agent design. CollabSkill provides a substantive disclosure about using coding agents, but no relevant evaluation argument or findings. No supplied source substantively opposes the proposition, yet the predominance of non-attributable bibliographic material means absence of opposition cannot be treated as support.
